Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 3:

﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself.﴾ That is because of what it contains of putting him at ease after alienation, and of turning toward him after aversion. It has also been said that the shift first to the third person (ghaybah, absence) and then to the second person (khitab, direct address) is to increase the rebuke. This is like one who complains to people about a wrongdoer who wronged him, and then turns toward the wrongdoer when the complainant's grief rises, confronting him with reproach and the establishing of proof. In mentioning the blind man there is something of this, for it is a description that suits turning toward him with kindness. Also in it is the removal of the notion that the address is restricted to a specific blind man, and an indication that every weak person deserves attention from one like himself, following the principle: "The judge should not judge while he is angry."

As for "an" (أنْ), it is with the omission of the preposition, namely the lam of causation, and it is governed by the first of the two verbs according to the preference of the Kufans, and by the second according to the preference of the Basrans. That is: he frowned because the blind man came to him, and he turned away on account of that.

The apparent view is that the clause is connected to the verb of knowing (al-diraya) in a way that takes the place of its object. That is: what makes you aware of the state of this blind man, perhaps he would purify himself by what he receives of the laws, from some of the filth of sin?

The purpose is to negate your knowledge that he would be purified or would be reminded. The expectation (al-tarajjī, "hope") refers either to the blind man or to the Prophet (ﷺ), according to what has been said. It indicates that the hope of his purification, or his being one from whom such a thing is hoped for, is sufficient to prevent frowning and turning away. How much more so when his seeking purification was certain. Because the expectation was attached to him rather than certainty, and his share was diminished, the object of purification was taken as "some of the impurities" (baʿḍ al-awḍār), as a reinforcement of this. In it there is also a display of what the station of majesty requires here: the purification is taken in its general sense and applied to whatever the word applies to, not only to its complete form.

Some have restricted the second to the case where what he learns is supererogatory, and the first to the case where it is otherwise. This, as you see, is not so.

In the verse there is an allusion and an indication that whoever among the disbelievers the Prophet (ﷺ) turned to for their purification and admonition, from them purification and remembrance are not expected at all. It is like your saying to someone explaining a matter to one who does not understand it, while he has another present who is capable of understanding it: "Perhaps this one understands what you are explaining." For he perceives that he intended to make another understand, and that he is not fit for what he intended.

It has been said: the allusion arises from the fact that the one spoken of was already purified of sins and admonished. And it has been said: the pronoun in ﴿laʿallahu﴾ refers to the disbeliever, and the expectation refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: you hoped for his purification through Islam and his remembrance through admonition, and for that reason you turned away from another. This view is deemed weak, because the disbeliever has not been mentioned previously, and because the pronoun is singular while the apparent reading is plural, that is, based on the well-known view that the one with whom the prayer and peace of Allah were occupied was a group. It is reported in some narrations that he was one person.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verses 11–12:

It is also permissible that it be an eloquent directive to abandon what he was reproached for (peace be upon him), based on the view that the revelation came during that conversation and before it had ended. In some reports it is said that after he (ﷺ) frowned at a poor man and did not attend to a rich man, the people learned good manners from this; it is related from Sufyan al-Thawri that the poor used to be princes in his assembly.

The second clause is a parenthetical insertion brought in to encourage the Qur'an and to urge its memorization or being admonished by it. The connection of the parenthetical clause with the fā' (fa, "so") has been explicitly stated by Ibn Malik in al-Tashil without reporting any disagreement about it. However, it has been objected that the transmission, because it contradicts that, is not established, and it is possible that among the people there was one who denied that, so he agreed with him at times and disagreed with him at others. How subtle is the statement of al-Sa'd in al-Talwih: "The parenthetical clause may occur with a waw or a fā'":

So know, for a person's knowledge benefits him.

That said, it has been said: the first pronoun refers to the surah or to the preceding verses, and the second to the reminder and the admonition, since it carries the meaning of remembrance and exhortation; or to the referent of the first, and the masculine form is in view of that being a Qur'an. This is preferred because it avoids resorting to interpretation before it is needed. It has been objected that this is not right: although the surah or the verses are characterized by the noble attributes that will come, God willing, they are not among what was cast upon the one who was made needless, and deserving of that is what will come, God willing, of invoking curses against him and wondering at his excessive disbelief, since they were revealed after the incident. It is also permissible that the two pronouns refer to the reproach that occurred, with the second masculine because it was a rebuke; but this is refuted by the description with the attributes that follow, though it may be possible if one considers that the rebuke occurred through the verses mentioned before, which are characterized by what was mentioned, as you have just heard. It has also been said: you may take them to refer to the call to Islam, with the second masculine because it was an invitation; but this, despite what is in it, is something the context rejects.

﴿Noble﴾, meaning: honoured with God, exalted in His presence, mighty and majestic. It is from *al-karamah* in the sense of reverence (*al-tawqir*). Or it means: kindly disposed toward the believers, asking forgiveness for them, guiding them by inspiration (*ilham*) to what is good, and descending with what completes them of the sacred laws (*shara'i*). In this sense it is from *al-karam*, the opposite of *al-lu'm* (baseness).

﴿Righteous﴾, meaning: pious (*atqiya'*). It is also said: obedient to God, Exalted is He, from the saying "So-and-so *yabarru* his Creator," i.e., obeys Him. It is also said: truthful, from "he *barra* in his oath" (fulfilled his oath). *Bararah* is the plural of *barr* only. As for *abrar*, it may be the plural of *barr*, like *rabb* and *arbab*, or the plural of *barr* (in the form of *ṣāḥib*, pl. *ṣaḥāb*)... though some grammarians forbade this because it is not consistent. According to what has been said, the first plural (*abrar*) is specific to the angels, and the second (*barara*) to humans in the Qur'an and in the language of the Lawgiver (ﷺ). This is because *abrar* belongs to the forms of paucity (*qillah*, the forms denoting small numbers), not *barara*, and the God-conscious angels are more numerous than the God-conscious humans. So it was fitting to use the form of paucity even though its literal sense is not intended for humans, and not for them. Al-Raghib said: He specified *barara* for them because it is more emphatic than *abrar*, since *barara* is the plural of *barr*, whereas *abrar* is the plural of *barr* being *bārr*, and *barr* is more emphatic than *bārr*, just as *adl* is more emphatic than *ʿādil*. He seems to mean that describing with *barr* is more emphatic, being of the kind of describing by a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), than describing with *bārr*. But you have heard that *abrar* may be the plural of *barr* just as it may be the plural of *bārr*. Also, whether the angels are more deserving of the more emphatic description, compared with humans in general, is open to discussion. It has also been said: *abrar* is more emphatic than *barara*, since it is the plural of *bārr*, and *bārr* is more emphatic than *barr* due to the increase in its morphological pattern. Since the attributes of perfection in the children of Adam may be complete or deficient, they were described as *abrar*, indicating praise of them with the most complete attributes. As for the angels, their attributes of perfection are never deficient, so they were described as *barara*, because it indicates the basic quality without regard to intensification, since they have no need of that, and as an indication of the excellence of humans, because in their being *abrar* there is striving and resistance against the call of natural inclination. There is in this what is not hidden. From the use of *barara* for the angels is what Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The one who recites the Qur'an while being proficient in it is with the noble, righteous scribes (*safarah*), and the one who recites it while finding it difficult has two rewards."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 17:

﴿Qutila al-insanu﴾ (Woe to man / "May man be destroyed") is a supplication against him with the most vile and dreadful of curses.

﴿Ma akfarahu﴾ ("How ungrateful he is!") is an expression of wonder at his excessiveness in ingratitude (kufran) and a statement of his deserving the supplication against him. What is meant by "man" here is either: a) the one who has become independent of the Noble Qur'an, whose sublime attributes, which call for turning towards it and believing in it, have been mentioned; or b) the species, in terms of its including him and his like among its individuals. This latter view is preferred, on the basis that the verse was revealed concerning what Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ikrimah regarding Utbah ibn Abi Lahab: he disowned his father, then embraced Islam; his father then reconciled with him, gave him wealth, and equipped him for Syria. He sent word to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I disbelieve in the Lord of the star when it sets." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, send Your dog upon him, until it devours him." When he was in the midst of the journey, he recalled the supplication, so he offered those with him a thousand dinars if he woke up alive. They made him sleep in the middle of the caravan with the baggage around him. A lion approached the camels, leapt, and was suddenly upon him, tearing him apart. His father would lament him, weep over him, and say: "Muhammad never said anything at all except that it came to pass."

Another account of this story, longer than this one, will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, so do not overlook it.

Furthermore, this is a statement of utmost concision. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: "You will not find a style harsher than it, more indicative of wrath, or further-reaching in blame, while its two extremities are close together, nor more comprehensive for the imams in its brevity, since it includes what you have heard of supplication, the intended meaning, for it is inconceivable that the Exalted would be subject to its implication, and in the intended wonder, since wonder is impossible for Him, glorified be He, it is a cause of wonder for every listener." Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The first clause indicates that they deserve the greatest kinds of punishment by custom, and the second is an alert that they have been characterized by the greatest kinds of vile and reprehensible deeds in the Law. This was not heard before the revelation of the Qur'an. As for what is attributed to Imru' al-Qays of his saying:

"A man wishes for winter in summer, but when winter comes he denies it,
He is never content in one state ∗∗∗ Man is destroyed, how ungrateful he is!"

it has no basis. Anyone with even minimal knowledge of the speech of the Arabs does not fail to recognize that the one who said this is a later poet who intended to borrow from the Qur'an, not a pre-Islamic (jahili) poet. Some have allowed that the Exalted saying ﴿Qutila al-insanu﴾ is a report that He will slay the disbelievers through the revelation of the verse of fighting, and that the past tense is used to emphasize that this will certainly occur; but this is not correct. Similar to this is what has been said, that ma is interrogative, meaning: "What thing has made him disbelieve?", that is, made him a disbeliever, in the sense that there is no thing that justifies his disbelieving.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verses 18–19:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of his excessive ingratitude, by detailing the countless blessings that Mighty and Majestic God bestowed upon him, from the beginning of his natural disposition (fitrah) to the end of his life, blessings which call for being met with gratitude and obedience, while he falls short of that. The interrogative (istifham) is said to be for belittlement (tahqir). The answer, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From a drop of seminal fluid He created him﴾, does not imply that it is a genuine answer, since it is not truly an answer; rather it is in its (interrogative) form, and it is a substitution (badal) for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ It is also permitted that it be for affirmation (taqrir) and belittlement, derived from the indefinite word "thing" (shay'). It is also said that belittlement is understood from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From a drop﴾ etc.; that is: from what despicable, contemptible thing did He create him? From a foul drop of seminal fluid did He create him.

﴿Then He measured him﴾: then He prepared him for what suits him and befits him, of limbs and forms. Thus, taqdir here means preparation for what is fitting. This is why it is appropriate that it be conjoined with "then" (fa) rather than "He proportioned" (taswiyah), because creation (khalq) in this sense means taqdir, or includes it, so "then" would not fit. It is also permitted that this be a detailed explanation of what was first stated in summary in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾; that is: then He measured him in stages until He perfected his creation.

It is also said that belittlement is understood from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From a drop﴾ etc.; that is: from what despicable, contemptible thing did He create him? From a foul drop of seminal fluid did He create him.

﴿Then He measured him﴾: then He prepared him for what suits him and befits him, of limbs and forms. Thus, taqdir here means preparation for what is fitting. This is why it is appropriate that it be conjoined with "then" (fa) rather than "He proportioned" (taswiyah), because creation (khalq) in this sense means taqdir, or includes it, so "then" would not fit. It is also permitted that this be a detailed explanation of what was first stated in summary in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾; that is: then He measured him in stages until He perfected his creation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 20:

﴿Then He made the way easy for him﴾. That is: then He facilitated his exit from the womb, as has come in a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, by opening the mouth of the womb, stretching the sinews along its path, and turning his head downward after it had been in the upward direction. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from Qatadah, Abu Salih and al-Suddi, the meaning of "the way" (al-sabil) is the way of upright reflection (al-nazar al-qawim) that leads to faith, and facilitating it for him is the bestowal of intellect (al-ʿaql) and enabling him to reflect. Mujahid, al-Hasan and ʿAta' said, and it is also a report from al-Habr (Ibn ʿAbbas): it is the way of guidance and misguidance; that is, He made easy for him the path he wishes to take, from the path of good and guidance and the path of evil and misguidance, by empowering him, exalted and majestic is He, over each of them and enabling him to it. And being empowered over what one wills is a manifest blessing, setting aside whether it is good or evil. So it is not objected that how can the facilitating of the path of evil and misguidance be counted among the blessings? It is said: it is counted among them because, if it were not made easy like the path of good, he would not deserve praise and reward for turning away from it. Its abandonment is based on the view that abandoning a forbidden act, such as fornication, when one lacks the ability to commit it, for instance due to impotence, is not rewarded for it. It is said, however: one is rewarded and praised for it if the abstainer, within himself, deems that were he able he would not have done it. Some of them said:

Inability to do evil is a blessing, and he recited:

"Since I have no power to harm people, that is my thanks for the blessing of being a man."

The word "the way" is in the accusative by an implied verb that the apparent one explains, and in it there is emphasis on facilitation and firm establishment in the soul through repetition. It was said: the definite article (al-) rather than an idafah (possessive construction) indicates its generality, for if it were said "his way" it would suggest distribution, that each person has a way specific to him. Some scholars restricted this subtle point to the last meaning of "the way," so reflect. On this meaning it was said: in it there is an allusion that the world is the way and another thing is the destination, since the verse indicates that what is facilitated is the path of the responsible, upon which reward and punishment are based. This is obscure. In any case, the pronoun in "made it easy for him" (yassarahu) refers to "the way," and there is no ambiguity in the separation, so that it would be a deficiency in exposition.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 21:

﴿Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave.﴾ That is, He made him one who has a grave, in which his corpse is concealed, as an honour to him, and He did not leave him cast upon the earth, where whoever sees him would find him repugnant, and where beasts of prey and birds would divide him among themselves when they came upon him, like the rest of the animals. What is meant by "making him one who has a grave" is that He, mighty and majestic, commanded his burial. It is said: qabara al-mayyit (he buried the dead) when he buried him with his own hand, and from this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Had she (the she-camel) propped a dead man against her chest, he would have lived and would not have been carried to the grave-digger."

And aqbarahu means: he commanded that he be buried, or enabled him to be buried. So in the verse there is an indication of the legality of burying a human being, and this is something on which there is no disagreement. As for burying other animals, it has been said that it is permissible (mubah), not disliked, and it may be sought for a lawful purpose that requires it, such as averting the harm of its carcass, for example. Counting death among the blessings is because it is, in general, a means to the eternal life and the lasting bliss. These blessings were singled out for mention because they contain a description of the states of the human being from his beginning to his end, and what they include of blessings that are pure bounty from God. So when the rational person reflects on this, he knows the ugliness of disbelief and of ingratitude for the blessings of the Lord, glorified and exalted, and so he thanks Him, mighty and exalted, through faith and obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 22:

﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him.﴾ That is: when He wills his raising (inshar), He raises him, according to the well-known rule concerning the omission of the object of the verb of willingness (mashi'ah). The linking of the raising (al-inshar) to His, the Exalted's, will indicates that its time is not specified at all; rather, it depends on His will. This is unlike causing death (al-imatah), for its time is specified in general terms, according to what is customary in natural lifespans. The situation is the same with the time of burial (al-iqbar), and it is even more evident in that case.

Shu'ayb ibn al-Hijab, as reported in the book al-Lawami', and Ibn Abi Hamzah, as reported in the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah, read: «nashara-hu» without a hamzah. Both are dialects (lughatan) for reviving (al-ihya').

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 80, verse 23:

The words of the Most High, ﴿Nay﴾, are a rebuke to man for his ingratitude for blessings, which has reached its extreme. His, glorified is He, words ﴿He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ are an explanation of the cause of the rebuke. The "lamma" (not yet) is a negating particle that governs the jussive, and its negation is not discontinued (i.e., it extends to the present). The "ma" is a relative pronoun, and the pronoun in "amarahu" (He commanded him) is either referring to man, like the concealed pronoun in "yaqdi" (he has fulfilled), with the returning pronoun to the relative pronoun being omitted, meaning "by it"; or it refers to the relative pronoun, by way of omission and connection, and the returning pronoun to man is omitted, meaning "it was said to him." The second is better, because the omission of the object is easier than the omission of the pronoun returning to the relative pronoun. The intended meaning of "what He commanded him" is all that He commanded him. The meaning, as said by more than one scholar, is: he has not fulfilled, from the beginning of his life, His obligation upon him until the time of his death and burial; or, from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until this end, despite the long span and its extension, all that He commanded him, so he has not come out of all of the Most High's commands, since no one is free from some shortcoming. This was narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah. In this view, the absence of fulfilment is taken as a negation of generality. It has been objected that there is no doubt that the context of the noble verses is to show the extreme magnitude of man's offence and the realization of his excessive ingratitude, which merits great wrath, and it is clear that this is not established by such a degree of shortcoming that none of its individuals is free from. It was chosen that the absence of fulfilment be taken as a general negation, either on the basis that the one judged is man who is self-sufficient, or that he is the kind, but not absolutely; rather, the fulfilment of the judgement of non-fulfilment concerns some of its individuals, and it has been ascribed to all, as in the words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful﴾. Or, on the basis that its fulfilment is all of it insofar as it is a whole, by way of lifting the universal affirmation but not the universal negation. The meaning is: none of its individuals has fulfilled what He commanded him, but some of them have failed in it through disbelief and disobedience, although what has been detailed of the various kinds of bounties that encompass all should mean that none of them differs from it. From al-Hasan: "Nay" means "truly", so it is connected to what follows; that is: truly he did not act upon what He commanded him. Ibn Furak said: the pronoun in "yaqdi" refers to God, the Most High; that is: God, the Most High, has not decreed for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith, but commanded him to establish proof against him, having not yet decreed it for him. Its remoteness is not hidden.

The apparent reading according to this is that "Nay" also means "truly".

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So let man look at his food﴾, in the sense of: if this is the state of man, that until now he has not fulfilled what He commanded him, although what the previous blessings require is that he fulfil it, then let him look at his food... etc. Perhaps he will fulfil it. In the Isami glosses (al-Hawashi al-'Isamiyya), it is not hidden what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾ of the complete stirring up of man and urging him to comply with what follows of the command to look. The subordinating of the command upon it is based on the fact that compliance, as it should be, becomes easy after he refrains from what he is engaged in. The apparent meaning is that by "man" here is meant something like what was meant in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Cursed is man﴾. When the author of the said glosses permitted interpreting the non-fulfilment as total negation, and made the discussion concern man who is extreme in disbelief, he said: so the referent of the pronoun in ﴿fulfil﴾ is other than the man who was commanded to look, for that one is general, and therefore it was made explicit. And what preceded contained a mention of the innate blessings, that is, what relates to the person's own self, its essence and its necessary attributes. This is a mention of the external blessings corresponding to those. It has been said: the first are particular blessings and the second are general blessings. It has also been said: those relate to origination and these relate to continuance, and this is open to scrutiny. The apparent meaning is that by "food" is meant what is eaten in its varieties, and it was restricted to it without mentioning drink, because the traces of power in it are more numerous than its traces in drink. As for the consideration of taghlib (the figure of speech in which one term is given precedence over its counterpart), what is wrong with it is not hidden.

[Page 46]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That We poured down the water﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). Because the water is one of the causes of its growth, it is as if it contains it. The returning pronoun (al-a'id) is omitted, meaning: We poured down water for it. It has also been permitted that it is a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull), with the sense: "Let man look at Our bounty in his food: that We poured down the water..." etc. As you see, this is weak. In any case, the object of the looking is the substitute (al-badal). By this, what is narrated from Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others is weakened: that the meaning is "Let him look at his food when it has become excrement, so that he may reflect on the end of the world and what its people covet." By my life, this meaning is far from the context, and I do not think that the soundness of their transmission from these eminent figures is agreed upon. The apparent sense of "pouring" (al-samb) requires restricting the water to rain, which is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, though some have permitted that the word is meant in a more general sense. They said: In every water there is a pouring from Allah, the Exalted, by His creating its causes upon the roots of plants. You know that the delivery of water to the roots of plants makes calling it "pouring" unlikely. The emphasis of the sentence is for the sake of attention to its content, while it is also liable to be denied by one of limited perception, because he does not sense an action from Allah, the Exalted. The attribution to Him, Mighty and Majestic, is known only through correct reflection.

Most readers recite «Inna» with a kasra, as a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani), as if, when He, Glorified be He, commanded looking at what Allah, Majestic and Exalted, has provided of kinds of food, it was asked: "How was that brought into being and created after it was not?" So it was said: "Inna sababna..." etc.

And the Imam al-Husayn ibn Amir al-Mu'minin 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face and be pleased with them both, recited «Anna sababna» with a fatha on the hamza and imala, with the meaning: "Let man look at how We poured down the water ﴿pouring﴾ wondrously."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verse 26:

﴿Then We split the earth﴾, i.e., with plant growth, as Ibn ʿAbbas said, ﴿splitting﴾ in a wondrous manner, fitting for what splits it of plants in smallness and largeness, form and shape.

It has been said: its splitting is by plowing (al-kirab), and attributing it to His Exalted pronoun is a metaphor of the type of attributing an action to its cause. Although Allah, Exalted and Majestic, is the originator in reality, it has been clarified in its proper place that the attribution of an action in its true sense is to the one who performs it, not to the one from whom it issues as bringing into being; and for this reason the active participle is derived for him. It has been objected that the word ﴿then﴾ (thumma) rules this out.

The *fa'* in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We caused grain to grow therein﴾, is used because the splitting of the earth, in the sense mentioned above, has no sequential relation to the rain at all, nor to the growing of the grain without any interval. The intended "growth" is what sprouts from the earth until the growth is complete and the grain forms. The splitting of the earth through the plants continues to increase and widen until it reaches that stage. Moreover, the purpose of the noble text is to explain the bounties that flow from His presence, Exalted is He, in a wondrous manner that goes beyond the customary habits, as is indicated by the pairing of the two verbs with their verbal nouns. Therefore, inserting the action of the Benefactor between the occurrence of those bounties disrupts the intended meaning, and there is room for debate on this.

It has also been objected that splitting the earth by plowing (*al-kirab*) does not appear in the cases of grapes, olives, and date palms. It has been answered that it is not a necessary requirement of coordination (*al-atf*) that the conjoined item be restricted by everything by which the item it is conjoined to is restricted. It is also possible that the mention of plowing in the objection was meant as an example, or that it was intended to include digging. It has also been permitted that the intended meaning is splitting the earth with springs, and that the pouring of water means the sending down of rain, and by this the rivers flow. But this has been challenged: it is contradicted by the sequence of the splitting upon the pouring of water with the particle indicating delay (*thumma*). Also, the arrangement of the growing upon the combination of the pouring and the splitting in the sense mentioned does not fit His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds pouring water﴾ ﴿That We may bring forth thereby grain﴾, and the verse that follows, because it implies that the pouring and the sending down of the rain are independent in that. It has been answered that the water of the springs is from the rain, not from the vapors trapped in the earth. But it is not hidden from anyone with insight that this answer is distant and forced.

The intended meaning of "grain" (*habb*) is the genus of grains by which people sustain themselves and which are stored, such as wheat, barley, maize, and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 80, verses 28–30:

﴿And grapes﴾ is well known. ﴿And fodder﴾: Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: it is al-fasfasa (clover). Al-Khalil restricted it to the fresh (green) kind and said: when it dries it becomes al-qatt (dry fodder). It was named by the verbal noun of qadabahu, meaning he cut it, in an intensive sense, as if the cutting itself is what is repeated and multiplied by its frequent cutting. Those who interpreted al-abb as something that includes this weakened this view. It was also said that it is everything that is cut off to be eaten by the son of Adam while still tender from plants, such as herbs and asparagus (al-hilyun).

In al-Bahr, from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas), it is said: it is the fresh (moist) kind, which is cut from the palm tree, and he took as supporting evidence its mention alongside grapes. What is in this is not hidden.

﴿And olives and date palms﴾: these are both well known. ﴿And gardens﴾: lush orchards. ﴿Dense﴾: that is, large. Its root is the plural of aghlab and ghalba', which describe a neck (meaning thick-necked). The term may also be applied to a man, but the first is the more usual use. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"He walks with them, thick-necked men, as though they were stallions, clad in dark camel-hair mantles."

The description of the gardens with this is by way of metaphor: the density of the leaves of the trees and their roots is likened to the thickness of the veins and the swelling of the sinews, together with the merging of some into others, in the thickness of the neck. However, the thickness in trees is stronger, because the matter is reversed when considering the merging and the strengthening of some by others until they become one thing. It is also permissible that there is here a metonymy (majaz mursal), as in al-marsin (the nose-ring), by intending by al-aghlab the thick in general. It is also treated as a figure in the predication, because the gardens themselves are not thick; rather, their trees are thick. Some said: what is meant by the gardens is the trees themselves, because of their place of conjunction with what is in the scope of "We caused to grow", so do not overlook this.

﴿And grass (abban)﴾. From Ibn 'Abbas and a group [of scholars]: it is pasture and herbage, from "when he sought it and aimed for it," because it is sought and aimed for; or from "abba li-kadha" when he prepared himself for such-and-such, because it is prepared pasture. *Our root is Qays, and Najd is our abode, and for us there is the abb therein and the watering place.*

Some have mentioned that what human beings eat of plants is called *al-hasidah* and *al-hasid*, while what other than them eat is called *al-abb*. On this is the saying of one of the Companions praising the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him:

*For him is a blessed supplication, whose wind is the east wind, by which Allah causes to grow the hasidah and the abb.*

'Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Dahhak that it is specifically straw (*tibn*). It has also been said that it is the dried fruit, because it is prepared (*yu'abbu*) and readied for winter, to be enjoyed as fruit. Abu 'Ubayd in his *Fada'il* and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibrahim al-Taymi who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the *abb*, what is it? He said: "What sky would shelter me, and what earth would carry me, if I say in the Book of Allah what I do not know?" Ibn Sa'd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and others related from Anas that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited on the pulpit: ﴿So We caused grain to grow therein﴾ ﴿and grapes﴾ – up to his saying – ﴿and grass (abban)﴾, and said: "All of this we know; but what is the abb?" Then he raised a staff that was in his hand and said: "By the life of Allah, this is indeed *al-takalluf* (artificiality). What harm is it to you, O son of Umm 'Umar, that you do not know what the abb is? Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book and act upon it, and what you do not know, leave it to its Lord."

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the narration of Anas as well, that he recited that and said: "What is the abb?" Then he said: "We were not charged with this," or "we were not commanded with this." From this there appears a prohibition on pursuing the meanings of the Qur'an and searching into its difficult matters. In *al-Kashshaf*: He did not mean that; rather, the people's greatest concern was devoted to action, and occupation with some knowledge that is not acted upon was considered artificiality. So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, intended that the verse is set forth as a favour upon man by way of what he desires and as a call to his gratitude; and it is known from its import that the abb is part of what Allah, glory be to Him, caused to grow for man as provision for him or for his livestock. So you should attend to what is more important than rising to thank Him, Mighty and Majestic, for what has been made clear to you; and do not let anything of what He has enumerated of His blessings be unclear to you, nor occupy yourself with seeking the meaning of the abb and knowing the particular plant that bears this name; be content with general knowledge until it becomes clear to you at another time." Then he enjoined people to proceed in this manner regarding similar difficult matters of the Qur'an. End of quotation.

This is the utmost that can be said in directing this matter. However, in some reports from al-Faruq, as in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, there is something which is far-fetched, if this interpretation is sound.

One point remains: it is fitting to note that the obscurity of the specific meaning of the abb to the two Shaykhs, may Allah be pleased with them, and to similar Companions, and likewise the disagreement about it, does not require that it be a rare word that damages eloquence, or that it was not used among the pure Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas explained it to Ibn al-Azraq as that which animals graze upon, and he cited as evidence the saying of the poet:

*You see among it the abb and the gourd mixed together.*

It occurs in the poetry of some Companions as you have heard; and whoever investigates will find otherwise.

Page 48

﴿A provision for you and your cattle.﴾ It has been said: it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu); meaning, He did that as a provision for you and your livestock. For some of the blessings enumerated are food for them, and some of them are fodder for their animals, and each is distributed and assigned according to what it requires. The shift (iltifat) serves to complete the enjoyment. Or it may be a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing its implied verb, with the extra letters removed; meaning, He provided you with that as a provision (mata'an). Or it may be a verbal noun governed by a verb that follows from it; meaning, you enjoyed that as a provision (mata'an), that is, enjoyment (tamatto'an). Or it may be a verbal noun not from its own root, since the three verbs mentioned are in the sense of giving enjoyment (al-tamti'), and the discussion of its counterpart has already passed, so reflect on this.

﴿So when the Shriek comes﴾ This begins the explanation of the conditions of their return (ma'ad) after the explanation of what relates to their creation and livelihood. The fa' (fa') indicates that what follows is consequent upon what the word "enjoyment" (matā') suggests of the swift passing of those blessings and the nearness of their dissolution. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the ghabarah is what descends to the ground, and the qatarah is what rises toward the sky, and the intended meaning is that the dust reaches their faces from above and from below. What is relied upon, however, is what preceded. Ibn Abi Abla read «قَتْرَةٌ» with a sukun on the ta' (qatrah). ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the owners of those faces, and the distance implied in it indicates the remoteness of their rank in wretched condition; that is, ﴿those who are described with what has been mentioned﴾. ﴿They are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾, that is, those who combine disbelief and wickedness. For this reason God, exalted is He, combined for them the ghabarah and the qatarah. It seems that the ghabarah corresponds to wickedness (fujur) and the qatarah to disbelief (kufur). We seek refuge in God, Mighty and Majestic, from that.
